extracted.intended_audience: students learning elementary combinatorics (high school / introductory undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook material on counting: definitions (lists, length, empty list), core counting principles (multiplication principle, permutations, combinations), factorials, Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem, with worked examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a list (ordered sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence of objects. A list is denoted by an opening parenthesis, followed by the objects, separated by commas, followed by a closing parenthesis. The objects are called the entries; the number of entries is the length of the list. Lists may have repeated entries. The empty list () is the unique list of length zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a, b, c, d, e); (5,3,5,4,3,3); (( ), ( ), ( )) where entries may themselves be sets or lists. Equality of lists requires exactly the same entries in exactly the same order, so rearrangement creates a different list. Warning: writing lists without commas/parentheses (e.g., 91011) can be ambiguous and lead to nonsense; use standard parenthesis/comma notation to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle (Fact 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose in making a list of length n there are a1 possible choices for the first entry, a2 possible choices for the second entry, a3 for the third, and so on. Then the total number of different lists that can be made is the product a1 · a2 · a3 · · · · · an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with a tree/branching diagram. Example: first entry from {a,b,c} (3 choices), second from {5,7} (2 choices), third from {a,x} (2 choices) gives 3·2·2 = 12 lists. Use this principle to model sequential choices where each position has a fixed finite number of options (possibly depending on earlier choices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition allowed vs not allowed (non-repetitive lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of list-counting problems: repetition allowed (same symbol may appear multiple times in different entries) and repetition not allowed (no repeated entries). A list in which repetition is not allowed is called a non-repetitive list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: license plates and telephone numbers allow repetition; drawing cards and lining them up (from a standard deck) produces non-repetitive lists because cards are distinct. The choice of model (allowing or forbidding repetition) changes the counting approach: with repetition use fixed choices per slot; without repetition use decreasing counts as symbols are used up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting lists with repetition allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: When repetition is allowed and each of k positions has a_i possibilities (often equal), the total number of lists is the product of the possibilities for each position (special case: if each position has n choices, number = n^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: length-4 lists from 7 symbols → 7^4 = 2401. License plates: 3 letters (26 choices each) followed by 4 digits (10 choices each) → 26^3 · 10^4 = 175,760,000. When counting lists with constraints (e.g., must contain at least one specific symbol), complementary counting (subtract lists without the symbol) is often effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting non-repetitive lists (permutations) and factorial connection
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of non-repetitive lists of length k chosen from n distinct symbols is n·(n−1)·(n−2)····(n−k+1), which can be written as n!/(n−k)!; in the special case k = n this equals n! (the number of permutations of n objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of non-repetitive length-4 lists from 7 symbols = 7·6·5·4 = 7!/(7−4)!. Use factorial notation to compactly represent products of consecutive integers. For permutations of all n symbols, n! counts the arrangements (0! defined as 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of factorial (Definition 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a non-negative integer n, n! (n factorial) is the number of non-repetitive lists of length n that can be made from n symbols. Thus 0! = 1 and for n > 1, n! = n·(n−1)·(n−2)····3·2·1. Also n! = n·(n−1)! (recurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table of small factorials: 0! = 1, 1! = 1, 2! = 2, 3! = 6, 4! = 24, 5! = 120, 6! = 720, etc. Argument that 0! must equal 1 so recurrence and counting interpretations remain consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding double-counting; careful case partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing possibilities into categories (e.g., by position of a symbol), ensure the categories are pairwise disjoint; otherwise lists may be counted multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: counting lists with repetition allowed that contain at least one E by summing counts for E-in-position-1, position-2, etc., overcounts lists where E appears multiple times (e.g., (E,E,A,B) belongs to multiple categories). Instead use complementary counting or inclusion–exclusion to avoid double-counting. The text demonstrates correct complementary method and incorrect naive summation that led to an overcount (1372 vs correct 1105).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the number of outcomes satisfying a property by subtracting the number of outcomes that do not satisfy the property from the total number of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: number of length-4 lists (repetition allowed) from 7 letters that contain at least one E equals total lists 7^4 minus lists with no E (6^4), giving 2401 − 1296 = 1105. This is often simpler than direct inclusion–exclusion when 'no occurrence' is easier to count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficient / combinations (Definition 3.2 and Fact 3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The binomial coefficient (n choose k) denotes the number of k-element subsets that can be chosen from an n-element set. For integers n, k with 0 ≤ k ≤ n, (n choose k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!). If k < 0 or k > n (or n negative) the value is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and small tables: (5 choose 3) = 10. Relationship to permutations: each k-element subset gives k! non-repetitive lists, hence number of k-element subsets equals number of non-repetitive k-lists divided by k!. Identity (symmetry): (n choose k) = (n choose n−k). Use this to count hands from a deck, lottery combinations, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's triangle and recurrence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange binomial coefficients in a triangular array (Row n lists (n choose k) for k = 0..n). Each entry satisfies (n+1 choose k) = (n choose k−1) + (n choose k) for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, which explains Pascal's triangle construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: when counting k-element subsets of an (n+1)-element set, partition by whether a particular element (e.g., 0) is included or not. Pascal's triangle rows correspond to coefficients of (x + y)^n. Construction: put 1s at ends of rows and each interior entry is the sum of the two entries above it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial Theorem (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-negative integer n, (x + y)^n = sum_{k=0}^n (n choose k) x^{n−k} y^k (i.e., the coefficients of (x+y)^n are the binomial coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation from Pascal's triangle and small expansions: (x+y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2, (x+y)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2 y + 3x y^2 + y^3, etc. The theorem connects combinatorial counts with algebraic expansion and justifies using binomial coefficients as expansion coefficients.
